https://macworld.com/article/3276314/pro.html:
Macworld

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t just the best display ever put in a laptop. It’s also Apple’s first-ever touchscreen in a Mac and the first time macOS has supported Touch as an input option. It’s a feature we longtime Mac users thought we’d never see, mostly because Apple has a history of saying it won’t happen.

But it has happened—and on the most expensive laptop Apple sells, no less. While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has plenty of other features to attract customers, which I will outline in my upcoming review, the touchscreen is one of the most interesting features to come to the Mac in years and is sure to be a major consideration for buyers when choosing which laptop to get.

However, macOS with Touch isn’t the same interface that you can just reach out to control with your fingers. Apple has enhanced and optimized macOS to accommodate Touch, making the overall experience satisfying. Here are my observations after spending a few days with it.

No lag or delay

Apple did not simply take a Touch input sensor, slap it on top of the OLED, pack it all up, and ship it. For the optimal experience, the Touch sensor is incorporated into the OLED panel, just as it is with the iPad Pro. That makes it perform more like a tablet than a usual touchscreen laptop.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

It also means there’s no lag when touching the screen. Tap the screen, and you’ll get an instant reaction from macOS: buttons, menus, sliders, icons, the Dock, you name it. Everything reacts the instant you touch it.

UI clarity

My major concern about the touchscreen MacBook Pro was whether Apple would do enough (or anything) to adjust macOS’s longstanding UI elements for Touch input. Some elements in macOS need to be larger to make them easier to touch; others need to be shifted to create more space; and still others need a complete rethink. A touch UI that demands cursor-style precision means you have to concentrate to do the most mundane of tasks. That’s tiring.

Foundry

In macOS 27.2 on the new MacBook Pro, Apple has enhanced macOS to accommodate Touch. Throughout the OS, elements appear when using Touch and return to the normal view when using a mouse or trackpad. The first thing you’ll notice is the set of traffic lights that appear in the upper right corner of windows to close, minimize, or expand windows full-screen, respectively. When tapped, the red, yellow, and green buttons magnify to make the target easier to hit.

Even menu items adjust by expanding a bit to add space between the items so they’re easier to tap with your finger. Another example is checkboxes, which let you tap on the accompanying text to select as well as the box itself.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

UI confusion

Almost all of the time, I can navigate through macOS just by using Touch. Apple thoughtfully considered the elements that I encountered to make them easy to touch, with one exception: video files. The ability to watch a tiny version of the video by clicking on the “Play” icon in the center of the video’s icon gets in the way of opening the file. Double-tapping to open the video file often resulted in the video playing in the icon, not actually opening the file. It’s one of the things that hasn’t been adjusted to accommodate Touch, and it needs a retool.

I also found that the mindset for Touch on macOS is separate from iOS. My experience with Apple’s touch-based UI is mostly with iOS, so I thought that macOS Touch would work similarly. But Apple decided to stick to macOS conventions, as illustrated by opening an app. In iOS, opening an app is a single tap. In macOS, a single tap selects the app, just as a single click does with a mouse or trackpad. You need to double-tap to launch the app.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Gesture support

Multi-Touch gestures on the Mac support the same gestures that are on the trackpad and, for the most part, your iPhone and iPad. It’s all smart and effortless, especially if you already use these gestures on a trackpad: Swipe with two fingers to scroll up, down, left, or right.  Use three fingers and swipe left or right to switch desktops. A four-finger swipe up opens Mission Control. A four-finger swipe down opens App Exposé, etc.

Pinch-to-zoom even works. Rotate, where you use two fingers in a rotating motion, also works, but this gesture was awkward for me to do on a standing screen. I think it’s easier to do on a trackpad or, say, an iPad that’s lying flat.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Screen wobble

Apple re-engineered the MacBook Pro’s hinge to make the screen more stable while touching it. The hinge provides enough resistance when you’re pressing relatively softly against the screen. Push hard enough, and the screen falls back, but most of the time, you’re not going to need to push that hard. In the animation above, you can see the screen wobble as I do the rotation gesture, but it’s exaggerated since I repeated the gesture several times and inadvertently pressed harder than usual.

If you tap lightly, you won’t see the display move, but most people will tap hard enough to see a wobble. However, my regular taps caused the display to shake slightly, which was noticeable but bearable. The wobble is significantly less than a regular MacBook Pro, however, and after the first few taps, I barely noticed it.

Fingerprints

It’s a consequence of using any touchscreen: the display will end up with fingerprints smeared all over it. Like an iPad, they’re not noticeable when the display is on, but when the display goes dark or turns off, ugh. It’s gross.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

This is just a fact about touchscreens we have to live with. Even with Apple’s oleophobic coating, there just isn’t a practical way to prevent fingerprints from appearing at all. There are personal habits that can be practiced to minimize the mess: clean your hands before using the touchscreen, wipe your hands frequently, don’t eat while using a touchscreen, etc. Or you could use touch-friendly gloves, or even wear latex gloves (I tried it and it works), but that’s not practical (and it’s ridiculous). Have a microfiber cloth handy to clean the display; Apple unfortunately doesn’t include one unless you spring for the nano-texture coating, but they sell one for $9. Amazon sells a six-pack of Koala Lens Cleaning Cloths for $10.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s Touch works only with fingers, not with an Apple Pencil or any third-party stylus. Other than fingerprints, using your fingers doesn’t offer nearly the same precision as using a stylus, so it’s closer to using an iPhone rather than an iPad or a graphics tablet.

A very good start

Apple isn’t marketing the MacBook Pro as a Touch-first device. Rather, Touch is something users can turn to when the situation calls for it. But it’s promising nonetheless. This first version of the Mac’s Touch UI is smooth, reliable, usable, and even fun. It’s a good start, and I hope Apple invents ways to take advantage of Touch, evolving it beyond being a touch interface on top of macOS.

But Apple decided to stick to macOS conventions, as illustrated by opening an app. In iOS, opening an app is a single tap. In macOS, a single tap selects the app, just as a single click does with a mouse or trackpad. You need to double-tap to launch the app.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Gesture support

Multi-Touch gestures on the Mac support the same gestures that are on the trackpad and, for the most part, your iPhone and iPad. It’s all smart and effortless, especially if you already use these gestures on a trackpad: Swipe with two fingers to scroll up, down, left, or right.  Use three fingers and swipe left or right to switch desktops. A four-finger swipe up opens Mission Control. A four-finger swipe down opens App Exposé, etc.

Pinch-to-zoom even works. Rotate, where you use two fingers in a rotating motion, also works, but this gesture was awkward for me to do on a standing screen. I think it’s easier to do on a trackpad or, say, an iPad that’s lying flat.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Screen wobble

Apple re-engineered the MacBook Pro’s hinge to make the screen more stable while touching it. The hinge provides enough resistance when you’re pressing relatively softly against the screen. Push hard enough, and the screen falls back, but most of the time, you’re not going to need to push that hard. In the animation above, you can see the screen wobble as I do the rotation gesture, but it’s exaggerated since I repeated the gesture several times and inadvertently pressed harder than usual.

If you tap lightly, you won’t see the display move, but most people will tap hard enough to see a wobble. However, my regular taps caused the display to shake slightly, which was noticeable but bearable. The wobble is significantly less than a regular MacBook Pro, however, and after the first few taps, I barely noticed it.

Fingerprints

It’s a consequence of using any touchscreen: the display will end up with fingerprints smeared all over it. Like an iPad, they’re not noticeable when the display is on, but when the display goes dark or turns off, ugh. It’s gross.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

This is just a fact about touchscreens we have to live with. Even with Apple’s oleophobic coating, there just isn’t a practical way to prevent fingerprints from appearing at all. There are personal habits that can be practiced to minimize the mess: clean your hands before using the touchscreen, wipe your hands frequently, don’t eat while using a touchscreen, etc. Or you could use touch-friendly gloves, or even wear latex gloves (I tried it and it works), but that’s not practical (and it’s ridiculous). Have a microfiber cloth handy to clean the display; Apple unfortunately doesn’t include one unless you spring for the nano-texture coating, but they sell one for $9. Amazon sells a six-pack of Koala Lens Cleaning Cloths for $10.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s Touch works only with fingers, not with an Apple Pencil or any third-party stylus. Other than fingerprints, using your fingers doesn’t offer nearly the same precision as using a stylus, so it’s closer to using an iPhone rather than an iPad or a graphics tablet.

A very good start

Apple isn’t marketing the MacBook Pro as a Touch-first device. Rather, Touch is something users can turn to when the situation calls for it. But it’s promising nonetheless. This first version of the Mac’s Touch UI is smooth, reliable, usable, and even fun. It’s a good start, and I hope Apple invents ways to take advantage of Touch, evolving it beyond being a touch interface on top of macOS.

What are they? Comfortable wireless over-ear headphones with excellent sound, improved noise cancellation, and long battery life.

Who are they best for? Travelers and frequent listeners seeking great sound and longer battery life for less than AirPods Max.

Who should skip them? Bargain hunters who can save with the Momentum 4, or buyers prioritizing the strongest noise cancellation.

The Momentum 4 was already one of our favourite over-ear headphones, and the new Momentum 5 provides a number of improvements that help to improve both sound quality and noise-cancellation. This update is a little more expensive though, now costing $399.95/£329.99, although the Momentum 4 is still widely available online with a reduced price of around $299.00/£199.00 so that’s still a good option if you’re looking for a bargain.

Available in a variety of colours, the Momentum 5 looks very similar to its predecessor, with large earpieces that house 42mm drivers and are thickly padded for comfort. Despite the large earpieces, the headphone only weighs 290g – compared to 386g for Apple’s AirPods Max – so they’re light and comfortable enough to wear for long periods of time, and Sennheiser also includes a sturdy travelling case to protect the headphones when you’re out and about. Battery life is impressive too, lasting for around 57 hours even when using noise-cancellation – compared to just 20 hours for the AirPods Max – which makes the Momentum 5 a great option for long journeys. And, if the battery does run down then you can switch to wired mode, with both USB-C and 3.5mm cables included (although the 3.5mm cable has a 2.5mm jack for connecting to the headphones, which could cause problems if you lose the cable and need to buy a replacement).

Bluetooth support has been updated for this model, stepping up to Bluetooth 5.4 and aptX Lossless/Adaptive, along with AAC for Apple devices, and support for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. The Momentum 5 is also certified for hi-res audio, and provides an impressive frequency response of 6Hz – 40KHz when using Bluetooth or a USB-C connection, which results in excellent sound quality.

It digs really deep for the rumbling electronic bass effects on Max Richter’s Shadow Journal, while the spatial audio creates an atmospheric soundstage for the track’s hazy, ambient sounds. There’s clarity on the higher frequencies too, with the violins cutting through haze to add a sense of urgency to the piece. Switching to something heavier and harder, the Momentum 5 does a great job of balancing the sonic mash-up of Sing Along by Sturgill Simpson. The fuzzy guitar riffs have a head-banging power that drives the track forward, while the precise, ticking percussion is irresistibly catchy. The synths wail with dance-floor energy, and the bass drop toward the end has a real kick to it.

The noise-cancellation has been improved as well. The Momentum 5 can now match the AirPods Max when it comes to blocking out low-frequency sounds such as the rumble of an aircraft engine. It does a good job with higher frequency sounds too, although the AirPods Max still has an edge in that area. Mind you, the AirPods Max are around $200/£200 more expensive so the Momentum 5 is really good value for money, especially with that outstanding battery life for long journeys.

Should you buy the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless?

The Momentum 5 Wireless is a strong choice if you want excellent sound, effective noise cancellation, and enough battery life for long journeys. Its deep, firm bass brings energy to electronic music and rock, while clear higher frequencies keep instruments distinct. The lightweight design and generous padding also make it comfortable for extended listening.

For Apple users, AAC support, Dolby Atmos spatial audio, and USB-C audio provide useful flexibility. Noise cancellation matches the AirPods Max for low-frequency rumble, although Apple’s headphones retain an advantage with higher-frequency sounds. The Momentum 5 counters with a considerably lower price and around 57 hours of battery life with noise cancellation enabled.

At $399.95/£329.99, it offers a compelling balance of sound, comfort, and endurance. However, bargain hunters should consider the Momentum 4, available for around $299/£199. The improved sound and noise cancellation make the newer model appealing, but the older headphones remain a good budget option.

Buying advice: What to look for when buying headphones

Below, we run through what to look for when choosing over-ear headphones for your iPhone or Mac, from sound quality and comfort to Apple features, lossless audio, noise cancellation and battery life.

Which headphone features matter for iPhone and Mac users?

Sound quality, comfort and reliable connectivity should come first. AAC support is useful for Bluetooth listening on Apple devices, but it isn’t required for basic compatibility. Check which additional features work with your iPhone, iPad and Mac, including easy pairing, automatic switching, hands-free Siri and Find My. These vary between models – even within Apple’s AirPods and Beats ranges.

Bluetooth multipoint lets compatible headphones maintain connections to two devices, making it useful for moving between an iPhone and Mac. Check how switching works in practice, rather than assuming it behaves like Apple’s automatic switching. Also check whether the manufacturer’s iPhone app offers equalizer controls and firmware updates.

Prioritize listening assessments over driver size or frequency-response claims. Look for clear vocals, audible detail and bass that suits your taste without overwhelming the music.

Can I listen to Apple Music lossless through headphones?

Yes, but the connection matters. Standard Bluetooth playback from an iPhone or Mac uses compression, even when you select a lossless track in Apple Music. A compatible wired connection is the straightforward way to hear lossless audio.

AirPods Max 2 and the first-generation USB-C AirPods Max support lossless playback over USB-C with current software and firmware. Some competing wireless headphones, including Beats Studio Pro, also offer USB audio. However, a USB-C charging port doesn’t necessarily support audio, so check before buying.

Traditional headphones with a 3.5mm plug are another option. Depending on your device, you may need an adapter or an external digital-to-analog converter (DAC). The supported resolution depends on the entire connection; wired listening doesn’t automatically guarantee support for Apple Music’s highest-resolution recordings. See our guide to DACs and lossless audio on iPhone and Mac.

Some headphones include a wireless transmitter. Check its compatibility and supported formats: adding a transmitter doesn’t automatically make playback lossless.

How much noise cancellation do I need?

For frequent flights, train journeys or noisy workplaces, prioritize effective active noise cancellation (ANC). It is particularly useful against steady sounds such as engine drone. Performance against conversations and sudden noises varies, so look for listening-test results rather than relying on manufacturers’ claims.

Passive isolation comes from the earcups sealing around your ears. A good fit helps both isolation and sound quality. Transparency or ambient modes use microphones to let you hear your surroundings without removing the headphones – useful when listening for announcements or maintaining awareness while walking.

If you make frequent calls, assess microphone performance separately: effective listening ANC doesn’t guarantee clear speech for the person you’re calling.

What makes over-ear headphones comfortable?

Comfort depends on weight, clamping pressure, headband design and earcup cushioning. Lighter headphones aren’t automatically more comfortable: how the headband distributes weight matters, too.

Look for enough adjustment to position the earcups comfortably around your ears, with a secure fit that doesn’t squeeze. Glasses can affect both comfort and the seal. Cushion materials also matter, particularly if heat and sweating become uncomfortable during longer sessions.

Try headphones for an extended session if possible, checking for pressure around your ears and across your head. For travel, consider whether they fold and whether the supplied case provides adequate protection.

How much battery life do I need?

Choose enough battery life for your longest listening sessions, with some allowance for missed charges. Around 30 hours with ANC enabled is a useful target for commuting and occasional travel, while frequent travelers may prefer longer endurance. A shorter runtime can still be sufficient if you recharge regularly.

Compare figures under the same conditions: turning off ANC can substantially increase battery life. Our reviews distinguish manufacturers’ estimates from measured results where available.

Quick charging can be as useful as total endurance, providing enough playback for a journey after a short charge. For longer trips, check whether headphones work while charging or through a cable with an empty battery. Wired listening doesn’t necessarily mean battery-free listening.

What is Auracast?

Auracast lets a compatible source broadcast audio to multiple headphones or hearing devices. It can be useful for shared listening or receiving audio in equipped public venues. Check explicitly for Auracast reception support; a recent Bluetooth version alone doesn’t guarantee it.

Buying advice: What to look for when buying headphones

Below, we run through what to look for when choosing over-ear headphones for your iPhone or Mac, from sound quality and comfort to Apple features, lossless audio, noise cancellation and battery life.

Which headphone features matter for iPhone and Mac users?

Sound quality, comfort and reliable connectivity should come first. AAC support is useful for Bluetooth listening on Apple devices, but it isn’t required for basic compatibility. Check which additional features work with your iPhone, iPad and Mac, including easy pairing, automatic switching, hands-free Siri and Find My. These vary between models – even within Apple’s AirPods and Beats ranges.

Bluetooth multipoint lets compatible headphones maintain connections to two devices, making it useful for moving between an iPhone and Mac. Check how switching works in practice, rather than assuming it behaves like Apple’s automatic switching. Also check whether the manufacturer’s iPhone app offers equalizer controls and firmware updates.

Prioritize listening assessments over driver size or frequency-response claims. Look for clear vocals, audible detail and bass that suits your taste without overwhelming the music.

Can I listen to Apple Music lossless through headphones?

Yes, but the connection matters. Standard Bluetooth playback from an iPhone or Mac uses compression, even when you select a lossless track in Apple Music. A compatible wired connection is the straightforward way to hear lossless audio.

AirPods Max 2 and the first-generation USB-C AirPods Max support lossless playback over USB-C with current software and firmware. Some competing wireless headphones, including Beats Studio Pro, also offer USB audio. However, a USB-C charging port doesn’t necessarily support audio, so check before buying.

Traditional headphones with a 3.5mm plug are another option. Depending on your device, you may need an adapter or an external digital-to-analog converter (DAC). The supported resolution depends on the entire connection; wired listening doesn’t automatically guarantee support for Apple Music’s highest-resolution recordings. See our guide to DACs and lossless audio on iPhone and Mac.

Some headphones include a wireless transmitter. Check its compatibility and supported formats: adding a transmitter doesn’t automatically make playback lossless.

How much noise cancellation do I need?

For frequent flights, train journeys or noisy workplaces, prioritize effective active noise cancellation (ANC). It is particularly useful against steady sounds such as engine drone. Performance against conversations and sudden noises varies, so look for listening-test results rather than relying on manufacturers’ claims.

Passive isolation comes from the earcups sealing around your ears. A good fit helps both isolation and sound quality. Transparency or ambient modes use microphones to let you hear your surroundings without removing the headphones – useful when listening for announcements or maintaining awareness while walking.

If you make frequent calls, assess microphone performance separately: effective listening ANC doesn’t guarantee clear speech for the person you’re calling.

What makes over-ear headphones comfortable?

Comfort depends on weight, clamping pressure, headband design and earcup cushioning. Lighter headphones aren’t automatically more comfortable: how the headband distributes weight matters, too.

Look for enough adjustment to position the earcups comfortably around your ears, with a secure fit that doesn’t squeeze. Glasses can affect both comfort and the seal. Cushion materials also matter, particularly if heat and sweating become uncomfortable during longer sessions.

Try headphones for an extended session if possible, checking for pressure around your ears and across your head. For travel, consider whether they fold and whether the supplied case provides adequate protection.

How much battery life do I need?

Choose enough battery life for your longest listening sessions, with some allowance for missed charges. Around 30 hours with ANC enabled is a useful target for commuting and occasional travel, while frequent travelers may prefer longer endurance. A shorter runtime can still be sufficient if you recharge regularly.

Compare figures under the same conditions: turning off ANC can substantially increase battery life. Our reviews distinguish manufacturers’ estimates from measured results where available.

Quick charging can be as useful as total endurance, providing enough playback for a journey after a short charge. For longer trips, check whether headphones work while charging or through a cable with an empty battery. Wired listening doesn’t necessarily mean battery-free listening.

What is Auracast?

Auracast lets a compatible source broadcast audio to multiple headphones or hearing devices. It can be useful for shared listening or receiving audio in equipped public venues. Check explicitly for Auracast reception support; a recent Bluetooth version alone doesn’t guarantee it.

How Macworld reviews headphones

When our audio experts review headphones our comprehensive evaluation covers sound quality, design and comfort, key features like noise cancellation, and overall value for money. We undertake subjective listening tests and an objective analysis of features and build quality.

The most critical aspect of our headphone reviews is an assessment of audio performance including Tonal Balance, Clarity and Detail, Audio Defects and Spatial Audio.

Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency Modes are also assessed, both being primary features users look for. We test how effectively the headphones block out different types of ambient sound, such as the low-frequency drone of an airplane engine versus higher-frequency chatter. We also assess how well transparency mode amplify outside sounds when you need to be aware of your surroundings.

Design, comfort and build quality are also important factors, as is the ease of use when it comes to the controls and functionality. Battery life is another important consideration, and the time it takes to charge the headphones.

Finally, we review the available connection options and the codecs supported since AAC support is required for Apple devices.

According to a research project by Derik Kauffman, Apple has a built-in list of words and phrases that the keyboard suggested words will never complete, and the swiping keyboard will not produce. This isn’t a censorship list—typing individual characters always works—but it can slow you down if you’re looking to use swiping or suggested words to speed up your iPhone typing.

The project is detailed at Swipeblocked.com, with additional code and data hosted on GitHub. There, Kauffman details his forensics to discover this feature and the blocked phrases.

Here’s how it works: Apple has built into iOS a hash table of “blocked” phrases. It’s not storing plain text of words, but rather matching hashes of word IDs to a set of banned hashes. If there’s a match, the iOS keyboard will not suggest the word. And if you are swiping, it will either input some other word for your swiped word or replace an earlier word in your phrase with a different word that has a similar swipe pattern.

The list of phrases has not been made public by Apple, and the company does not disclose how it chooses what goes on it. Kauffman reverse-engineered it from the hash table within iOS.

The phrases are mostly what you would expect. They include vulgarities, politically and socially charged phrases, rascist terms, various forms of bigotry, and so on. You can literally type out the phrase, “smoking weed,” but if you type “smoking wee…” then the keyboard suggestions to finish off that second word will never include the obvious “weed.” Instead, you’ll get “weekend” or “weekly.” And if you’re using Apple’s QuickPath (Slide to Type), you’ll get “smoking Wed” or some other word, no matter how precise you are about swiping the word “weed” correctly.

The Swipeblocked site has a list of all the English-language banned phrases in iOS 27. Warning: Many of them are not safe for work and highly offensive. But some are things that you may very well wish to type or swipe, especially in a particular context (illegal immigrant, NBA surveillance, etc.), and the refusal of the iOS keyboard to complete swiping entry or suggest the natural next word is one reason users are frustrated with it.

In addition to the phrases that are blocked from the suggested word area or swiping, there is a mechanism to prevent the autocomplete and suggested word list from suggesting individual words. The iOS dictionary labels words as either vulgar, offensive, or sensitive. Vulgar words are not suggested until the user manually types them three times. Offensive words are never suggested or completed by swiping (though you can always type them out yourself). Sensitive words are similarly never offered as a prediction or completion, and some of them can’t be swiped.

Why does Apple do all this? It’s likely less about policing your speech than it is about avoiding lawsuits and bad PR. All it takes is one person posting a screenshot of the iOS keyboard suggesting the word “good” after they type “The Nazis were” or “real” after Santa isn’t” (both included in the list) to cause a bad viral moment criticizing Apple’s intentions, even if the keyboard suggestions would only suggest things that the user had typed several times before.

However, it’s still overreaching. A good solution would be to give users a choice. Allow a keyboard setting, enabled by default, to moderate the suggested word list and swipe keyboard to avoid offensive content, but also give users the ability to turn it off. But until then, you’ll need to type a little more slowly if you want to write certain phrases.

What is it? A compact, mains-powered wireless speaker with lively sound, AirPlay 2, Bluetooth, and multiroom support.

Who is it best for? Apple users seeking an affordable speaker for a desk or shelf, with options for stereo pairing and multiroom expansion.

Who should skip it? Anyone wanting powerful deep bass, wired audio inputs, Dolby Atmos, or battery-powered portability.

We liked JBL’s Authentics range of speakers, but they were fairly expensive and the company seems to be phasing them out as it introduces an entirely new range of wi-fi speakers called Cove, which are a little more affordable and which seem to be taking over as JBL’s main option for multi-room audio. Prices start at $229.95/£199.99 for the entry-level Cove M1 that we test here, but there’s a more powerful model called the X1 available for $449.95/£429.99, and a portable model with a rechargeable battery, called the P1, priced at $399.95/£399.99.

Available in black or white, the mains-powered M1 is compact enough to sit easily on a desk or shelf, standing just 184mm high and 125mm wide and deep. It packs plenty into that compact design, though, with three 20mm high-frequency tweeters, and a larger 105mm woofer to handle lower frequencies. There are plenty of other features too, with both Bluetooth and dual-band Wi-Fi available for streaming music, and support for AirPlay 2 (although it’s a shame that there’s no 3.5mm socket or USB-C for a wired audio connection). The M1 has a built-in microphone as well, although this only works with Amazon’s Alexa, but there’s a switch that lets you turn the mic off if you prefer.

Setting it up

Getting started is very straightforward as the JBL One app initially uses Bluetooth to connect to the M1 and then prompts you to enter your wi-fi password to connect it to your home network. After that you can forget about the app and just use the M1 like any other AirPlay speaker. And, as well as supporting multi-room audio, you can pair two of the M1 speakers together for stereo sound, or use them with JBL’s MK2 soundbars for a home cinema set-up.

Sound quality

The M1 sounds pretty good on its own, though. The compact speaker doesn’t support Dolby Atmos – that’s only available in the larger P1 and X1 models – but it does a good job at evoking the hazy, ambient sound of Madonna’s Frozen. There’s a soft, warm tone to the opening strings, and a delicate touch on the electronic chimes that hang gently in the air. Then the percussion cracks like a whip, and the chugging guitar riff provides the energy that drives the song forward.

It can handle harder sounds too, wallowing in the fuzz-drenched guitars on Sturgill Simpson’s Sing Along. There’s an infectious, dancefloor energy to the wailing electronic keyboards, and the crisp percussion sets the pace with a foot-tapping rhythm. The M1 proves to be surprisingly powerful too, with 110W output that is more than loud enough for Sturgill’s stomper at just 50% of maximum volume, so there’s plenty more power available if you want to get things going at a party or BBQ.

The only slight weakness is the M1’s bass output. To be fair, it manages to reach down for the bouncing bass that kicks off Bad Guy by Billie Eilish, but the really deep electronic bass at the end of the song is more of a challenge and lacks the taut bass pulse that a larger speaker can deliver. Even so, the M1 performs well for a compact speaker in this price range, and the larger P1 and X1 models will be available soon if you need an even weightier sound.

The JBL Cove M1 delivers lively, detailed sound and impressive volume from a compact design that fits comfortably on a desk or shelf. AirPlay 2, Bluetooth, and straightforward setup make it an appealing choice for Apple users, while stereo pairing and multiroom support provide room to expand. Deep bass lacks the weight and precision of larger speakers, and there are no wired audio inputs. However, at $229.95/£199.99, it offers an attractive balance of sound quality, flexibility, and size. Choose it for everyday listening in smaller spaces, especially if you want an AirPlay speaker with plenty of energy and useful versatility.

If you usually spend your post-meal time falling asleep to A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving, you won’t find it on the usual broadcast or cable channels–it’s exclusively on Apple TV.

Before you wave that turkey drumstick in the air and curse the state of television and all the darn streaming services you need subscriptions for—yes, I’m talking about you, Uncle Fred—you don’t need a subscription to Apple TV to watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving. Apple is making the show available to anyone for a limited time. If you are an Apple TV subscriber, however, you can watch it anytime.

How to watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving for free on Apple TV

On November 15 and 16, anyone with an Apple ID can watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving. If you own an Apple device, you have one, but if not, Apple IDs are free and you don’t need a credit card to sign up. Once you have signed up, you can watch in several ways:

  • Through the TV app on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
  • On smart TVs with the Apple TV app.
  • On the web at tv.apple.com.
  • On an Apple TV device.

As we noted when Apple did this same deal with It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, Apple has all the classic Peanuts specials for the holiday season that used to air over broadcast TV. Apple TV also has A Charlie Brown Christmas that will have its free airing on Dec. 12 and 13. Apple TV also has Happy New Year, Charlie Brown but it is not listed as free-to-view.

A few years ago, Apple acquired the rights to the Peanuts cartoon series that stars Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus, Lucy, and other memorable characters. Since then, Apple has aired new Peanuts shows such as The Snoopy Show and Snoopy in Space, and new movies, including Peanuts in Space: Secrets of Apollo 10, Lucy’s School, and It’s the Small Things, Charlie Brown.

The Apple TV subscription streaming service is $14.99/£9.99 per month. Apple TV is also included in the Apple One subscription bundles, which include other Apple services, such as Apple Music, Apple News+, and iCloud storage. Apple One bundles are priced between $21.95/£18.95 and $39.95/£36.95 per month.
